prompt: Which IEEE standard family defines wireless LANs?
rejected: IEEE 802.3.

prompt: Which layers of the TCP/IP model does 802.11 define?
chosen: Layers 1 and 2, the same as Ethernet.
rejected: Layers 1 through 3, including addressing.

prompt: Do Layers 3 and above change when using wireless instead of wired?
chosen: No. Thanks to the modular nature of the TCP/IP model, they operate identically regardless of the Layer 1 and 2 protocols.
rejected: Yes. Wireless networks use a different IP addressing scheme at Layer 3.

prompt: Is Wi-Fi an official IEEE name?
chosen: No. It is a trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance, an organization that tests and certifies equipment for 802.11 compliance.
rejected: Yes. Wi-Fi is the IEEE's marketing name for the 802.11 family of standards.

prompt: What is the purpose of Wi-Fi certification?
chosen: To ensure interoperability between different vendors' devices.
rejected: To guarantee that a device meets minimum data rate requirements.

prompt: What is a bounded medium?
chosen: One where signals are confined to the cable, like copper or fiber, giving a controlled pathway for transmission.
rejected: One where signals radiate freely in all directions from the source.

prompt: Why is air called an unbounded medium?
chosen: Wireless signals propagate freely in open space, radiating in all directions from the source rather than being confined.
rejected: Because the range of a wireless signal has no theoretical limit.

prompt: What are the security implications of an unbounded medium?
chosen: All devices within range receive the signals, so data privacy is a greater concern and communications are usually encrypted even within the LAN.
rejected: None, since only the device the frame is addressed to will process it.

prompt: What wired device is wireless communication often compared to?
chosen: An Ethernet hub, because all devices connected to a hub receive all frames, just as all devices in range receive a wireless signal.
rejected: An Ethernet switch, because both forward frames only to the intended recipient.

prompt: Why must wireless devices operate in half duplex?
chosen: Only one device can transmit at a time on the shared medium, or the signals will collide.
rejected: Because wireless radios can only be tuned to transmit or receive, never built to do both.

prompt: Why are wireless networks usually slower than wired ones?
chosen: Their half-duplex nature means devices must contend for airtime, while switched wired networks operate in full duplex.
rejected: Because radio waves travel more slowly than electrical signals in copper.

prompt: What collision protocol do wired devices on a hub use?
chosen: CSMA/CD, Carrier-Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection.
rejected: CSMA/CA, Carrier-Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance.

prompt: What collision protocol do wireless devices use?
chosen: CSMA/CA, Carrier-Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance.
rejected: CSMA/CD, Carrier-Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection.

prompt: How does CSMA/CA work?
chosen: Before transmitting, a device listens to see if the channel is free. If it is busy, the device waits a short random period and checks again.
rejected: The device transmits immediately and listens for a collision, retransmitting if one is detected.

prompt: Does CSMA/CA prevent all collisions?
chosen: No. If two devices happen to transmit at the same time the frames can still collide, and they will have to retransmit.
rejected: Yes. That is the point of collision avoidance, unlike collision detection.

prompt: What can cause interference with a wireless LAN?
chosen: Neighboring wireless LANs on the same or overlapping frequencies, and devices like microwave ovens, cordless phones, and Bluetooth devices.
rejected: Only other 802.11 networks, since nothing else transmits in these bands.

prompt: Why are wireless communications regulated?
chosen: To manage the electromagnetic spectrum and prevent interference between different services such as cellular, satellite, and wireless LANs.
rejected: To ensure every vendor's equipment supports the same maximum data rates.

prompt: What is the FCC?
chosen: The US Federal Communications Commission, the regulatory body that governs radio frequency use in the United States.
rejected: The international body that coordinates frequency allocation across all countries.

prompt: What is the ITU?
chosen: The International Telecommunications Union, which works to coordinate the allocation of radio frequency spectrum across countries.
rejected: The organization that certifies wireless equipment as Wi-Fi compliant.

prompt: Can wireless equipment be used in any country?
chosen: No. Regulations differ between countries, so equipment legal in one country may be prohibited in another.
rejected: Yes, as long as it is Wi-Fi certified by the Wi-Fi Alliance.

prompt: What is free-space path loss?
chosen: The loss of signal strength as wireless signals propagate through space.
rejected: The loss of signal strength caused by walls and other physical obstacles.

prompt: How far does a wireless signal typically travel indoors?
chosen: Up to about 150 feet, or 46 meters, though it varies greatly with frequency, transmitter power, antenna type, and obstructions.
rejected: Up to about 300 feet, or 91 meters, which is the same indoors and outdoors.

prompt: How far can a wireless signal travel outdoors?
chosen: It can extend beyond 300 feet, or 91 meters, depending on conditions.
rejected: It is limited to the same 150 feet as indoors, because of free-space path loss.

prompt: What is absorption?
chosen: When a wave passes through a medium and is converted into heat, weakening the signal.
rejected: When a wave bounces off a surface rather than passing through it.

prompt: What is attenuation?
chosen: The weakening of a signal.
rejected: The bending of a signal as it passes between media.

prompt: What is reflection?
chosen: When a wave bounces off a surface rather than passing through it, as light does off a mirror.
rejected: When a wave bends around the edge of an obstacle.

prompt: Why is wireless reception poor in elevators?
chosen: Reflection. The signal bounces off the metal and very little penetrates inside.
rejected: Absorption. The metal converts the entire signal into heat.

prompt: What is refraction?
chosen: When a wave passes from one medium into another of different density, changing its speed and causing it to bend.
rejected: When a wave spreads out erratically after hitting an irregular surface.

prompt: Give an everyday example of refraction.
chosen: An object in water appearing shifted when viewed from above, because light bends as it moves from water to air.
rejected: A radio signal reaching around the corner of a building.

prompt: What is diffraction?
chosen: The bending and spreading of waves around the edges of an obstacle.
rejected: The conversion of a wave's energy into heat as it passes through a wall.

prompt: Why is diffraction useful in wireless networks?
chosen: It enables communication even without a clear line of sight, letting signals reach street level and indoor areas out of direct view.
rejected: It focuses the signal into a narrow beam, extending its range.

prompt: What is scattering?
chosen: When a wave hits a surface or medium with irregularities that make it spread out erratically.
rejected: When a wave splits into two waves of different frequencies.

prompt: What commonly causes scattering?
chosen: Dust, smog, water vapor, and textured surfaces.
rejected: Metal surfaces and dense concrete walls.

prompt: How does a device create a wireless signal?
chosen: It applies an alternating electric current to an antenna, which produces fluctuating electromagnetic fields that radiate out as waves.
rejected: It converts digital bits into light pulses that are emitted by the antenna.

prompt: What is amplitude?
chosen: The maximum strength of a wave's electric and magnetic fields, associated with how much energy the wave carries.
rejected: The number of times a wave's fields oscillate per second.

prompt: What happens if a signal's amplitude is too low?
chosen: The receiver will not be able to distinguish a coherent message from the signal.
rejected: The signal will arrive too quickly for the receiver to decode.

prompt: What is frequency?
chosen: How quickly the strength of a wave's electric and magnetic fields oscillates, measured in hertz, meaning oscillations per second.
rejected: The maximum strength reached by a wave's electric and magnetic fields.

prompt: How many hertz is one gigahertz?
chosen: 1,000,000,000 Hz, or one billion cycles per second.
rejected: 1,000,000 Hz, or one million cycles per second.

prompt: What is a wave's period?
chosen: The amount of time it takes for one full oscillation.
rejected: The total time a transmitter spends sending one frame.

prompt: What is the period of a 4 Hz wave?
chosen: 0.25 seconds.
rejected: 4 seconds.

prompt: Can two waves have the same amplitude but different frequencies?
chosen: Yes. Amplitude and frequency are independent characteristics.
rejected: No. A higher frequency always means a lower amplitude.

prompt: What are the advantages of higher frequencies in wireless LANs?
chosen: They typically support higher data transfer rates and are less crowded with other wireless devices.
rejected: They penetrate walls better and cover larger distances.

prompt: What are the advantages of lower frequencies?
chosen: They penetrate better through obstacles and can cover larger distances.
rejected: They support higher data rates and are less prone to interference.

prompt: What is the electromagnetic spectrum?
chosen: The entire range of electromagnetic radiation, including radio, ultraviolet light, X-rays, and gamma rays.
rejected: The range of frequencies set aside by regulators for wireless communication.

prompt: What frequency range is radio frequency?
chosen: Roughly 20 kHz to around 300 GHz.
rejected: Roughly 2.4 GHz to 6 GHz.

prompt: What is a band?
chosen: A specific range of frequencies, such as the AM radio band or the 802.11 wireless LAN bands.
rejected: A smaller division within a channel, used by one device at a time.

prompt: What is a channel?
chosen: A specific range of frequencies within a band. You can think of it as a smaller division of a band.
rejected: The physical path a signal takes between a client and an access point.

prompt: Which three RF bands are used for wireless LANs?
chosen: The 2.4 GHz band, the 5 GHz band, and the newer 6 GHz band.
rejected: The 900 MHz band, the 2.4 GHz band, and the 5 GHz band.

prompt: When was the 6 GHz band introduced to wireless LANs?
rejected: In 2013, alongside 802.11ac.

prompt: How many channels does the 2.4 GHz band have?
What is the standard channel width in the 2.4 GHz band?
chosen: 20 MHz, although older standards use 22 MHz.
rejected: 40 MHz, although older standards use 20 MHz.

prompt: Are all 14 channels of the 2.4 GHz band usable everywhere?
chosen: No. The US and Canada commonly allow only 1 to 11, most countries allow 1 to 13, and channel 14 is only permitted in Japan with an older standard.
rejected: Yes. The IEEE standardized all 14 channels for worldwide use.

prompt: What is the main problem with 2.4 GHz channels?
chosen: There is significant overlap between them, so adjacent APs can interfere with each other.
rejected: There are too few of them, so every AP in a building must share one.

prompt: Which 2.4 GHz channels should be used to avoid overlap?
What alternative 2.4 GHz channel layout is possible in some countries?
chosen: 1, 5, 9, and 13, in countries that allow up to channel 13.
rejected: 2, 7, and 12, in countries that allow up to channel 13.

prompt: What happens if adjacent APs use the same channel?
chosen: Devices have to contend for airtime not only with other clients of their own AP but with the clients of the neighboring AP too.
rejected: The two APs automatically merge into a single extended service set.

prompt: Why is the 2.4 GHz band often crowded?
chosen: It is used by many other technologies, including Bluetooth, microwave ovens, and cordless phones.
rejected: Because it has more channels than the other bands, so more devices are drawn to it.

prompt: What is the advantage of the 2.4 GHz band?
chosen: Its lower frequency gives better penetration through obstacles than the 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands.
rejected: Its channels are non-overlapping, which simplifies channel planning.

prompt: What range does the 5 GHz band cover?
chosen: Approximately 5.150 to 5.895 GHz, depending on the country.
rejected: Exactly 5.0 to 6.0 GHz in every country.

prompt: How do 5 GHz channels differ from 2.4 GHz channels?
chosen: They are non-overlapping at the standard 20 MHz width, which simplifies channel selection when deploying multiple APs.
rejected: They overlap even more than 2.4 GHz channels, so careful planning is essential.

prompt: What widths can 5 GHz channels be combined into?
What is the trade-off of using wider channels?
chosen: Higher data transfer rates, but fewer available channels.
rejected: Longer range, but more interference from neighbouring networks.

prompt: What is the downside of 5 GHz signals?
chosen: They do not penetrate walls and other barriers as well as 2.4 GHz, which can limit the coverage area.
rejected: They are far more crowded with household devices than 2.4 GHz.

prompt: Is poor penetration always a disadvantage?
chosen: No. It also means 5 GHz signals from neighbouring rooms and buildings are less likely to cause interference.
rejected: Yes. There is no situation where a weaker signal helps a wireless network.

prompt: What range does the 6 GHz band cover?
chosen: 5.925 GHz to 7.125 GHz. Both its low and high ends are outside the literal 6 GHz range.
rejected: Exactly 6.0 GHz to 7.0 GHz.

prompt: What channel widths does the 6 GHz band support?
chosen: A standard 20 MHz, combinable into 40, 80, 160, or even 320 MHz.
rejected: A standard 40 MHz, combinable into 80, 160, or 320 MHz.

prompt: What is the advantage of the 6 GHz band?
chosen: It provides even more non-overlapping channels than 5 GHz and is expected to relieve congestion and support greater data rates.
rejected: It penetrates walls better than either of the other two bands.

prompt: Which standards introduced the 6 GHz band?
chosen: 802.11ax, known as Wi-Fi 6E, and the newer 802.11be, known as Wi-Fi 7.
rejected: 802.11ac, known as Wi-Fi 5, and 802.11ax, known as Wi-Fi 6.

prompt: Which band does 802.11b use?
chosen: 2.4 GHz.
rejected: 5 GHz.

prompt: Which band does 802.11a use?
chosen: 5 GHz.
rejected: 2.4 GHz.

prompt: Which band does 802.11g use?
chosen: 2.4 GHz.
rejected: 5 GHz.

prompt: Which bands does 802.11n use, and what is its Wi-Fi name?
chosen: 2.4 and 5 GHz. It is Wi-Fi 4.
rejected: 5 GHz only. It is Wi-Fi 5.

prompt: Which band does 802.11ac use, and what is its Wi-Fi name?
chosen: 5 GHz. It is Wi-Fi 5.
rejected: 2.4 and 5 GHz. It is Wi-Fi 4.

prompt: What bands does 802.11ax use?
chosen: 2.4 and 5 GHz as Wi-Fi 6, plus 6 GHz as Wi-Fi 6E.
rejected: Only 6 GHz, which is why it is called Wi-Fi 6.

prompt: What is 802.11be?
chosen: Wi-Fi 7, which uses the 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz bands.
rejected: Wi-Fi 6E, which uses only the 6 GHz band.

prompt: Are the maximum rates listed for 802.11 standards realistic?
chosen: No. They are theoretical maximums under ideal conditions. Real-world rates are lower.
rejected: Yes. They are the rates measured in typical office deployments.

prompt: What is a service set?
chosen: A group of devices operating on the same wireless LAN, sharing the same SSID.
rejected: A group of access points that share a single wired uplink.

prompt: What is an SSID?
chosen: A service set identifier, a human-readable label that identifies the service set.
rejected: A unique hardware identifier assigned to each access point's radio.

prompt: What are the four main types of service set?
chosen: IBSS, BSS, ESS, and MBSS.
rejected: BSS, ESS, DS, and BSA.

prompt: What is an IBSS?
chosen: An independent basic service set, also called an ad hoc network, where wireless devices communicate directly with each other without an access point.
rejected: An isolated basic service set, where one AP serves clients with no connection to a wired network.

prompt: What is an IBSS good for?
chosen: Quick, temporary setups such as file sharing or gaming. It does not scale beyond a few devices.
rejected: Large enterprise deployments, since it needs no infrastructure.

prompt: What is a BSS?
chosen: A basic service set, the fundamental building block of a wireless LAN, where clients connect through a single access point.
rejected: A broadcast service set, where all clients in range receive every frame directly.

prompt: Can two clients in a BSS talk directly to each other?
chosen: No. They must send their frames to the AP, which relays them to the destination, even if they are in range of each other.
rejected: Yes, as long as they are within range of each other's signals.

prompt: What is a BSA?
chosen: A basic service area, the coverage area around an AP where clients can successfully communicate with it. Also called a cell.
rejected: A basic service address, the MAC address that identifies the AP's radio.

prompt: What is a wireless client?
chosen: Any device that connects to a wireless LAN via an AP.
rejected: Any wireless-capable device, including access points.

prompt: What is a station in 802.11 terminology?
chosen: Any wireless-capable device, including both clients and APs.
rejected: Only an access point, which serves the client stations around it.

prompt: Do SSIDs have to be unique?
chosen: No. Multiple BSSs may share the same SSID, which is how an extended service set is formed.
rejected: Yes. Two networks with the same SSID would be indistinguishable to clients.

prompt: What is a BSSID?
chosen: A basic service set identifier, which uniquely identifies a BSS. It is usually the MAC address of the AP's radio.
rejected: The human-readable network name that users select when connecting.

prompt: Can one AP provide more than one BSS?
chosen: Yes. For example, an enterprise might create one BSS for staff and one for guests with different security policies.
rejected: No. Each BSS requires its own physical access point.

prompt: Does creating multiple BSSs on one radio relieve congestion?
chosen: No. All the BSSs on one radio share the same channel, so all clients still contend for the same airtime.
rejected: Yes. Each BSS gets its own share of the channel, so congestion is halved.

prompt: How does an AP get a unique BSSID for each of its BSSs?
chosen: Usually by incrementing the radio's MAC address by 1 for each new BSS.
rejected: By generating a random MAC address for each BSS at startup.

prompt: Why do many modern APs have multiple radios?
chosen: So they can provide BSSs on different channels, typically one in the 2.4 GHz band and one in the 5 GHz band.
rejected: So they can transmit and receive at the same time, achieving full duplex.

prompt: What is the distribution system?
chosen: The wired network infrastructure that 802.11 connects wireless LANs to.
rejected: The system an AP uses to distribute frames among its wireless clients.

prompt: What happens without a distribution system?
chosen: An AP's wireless clients can only communicate among themselves, with no gateway to other networks.
rejected: The AP cannot form a BSS at all, since it has no way to advertise its SSID.

prompt: How does an AP connect to the distribution system?
chosen: Through its Ethernet port, usually via a switch.
rejected: Through a second wireless radio dedicated to the uplink.

prompt: What role does an AP play between the two media?
chosen: It acts as a bridge, translating 802.11 frames from wireless clients into Ethernet frames for the wired LAN, and vice versa.
rejected: It acts as a router, forwarding packets between the wireless subnet and the wired subnet.

prompt: How does an AP relate SSIDs to the wired network?
chosen: It maps each wireless SSID to a VLAN on the wired Ethernet network.
rejected: It assigns each SSID its own IP subnet and routes between them.

prompt: What is an ESS?
chosen: An extended service set, which links multiple BSSs through a distribution system to expand coverage.
rejected: An enhanced service set, where one AP uses multiple radios to serve more clients.

prompt: How are SSIDs and BSSIDs used in an ESS?
chosen: All the BSSs share the same SSID, but each has its own unique BSSID.
rejected: Each BSS has its own SSID, but they share a common BSSID.

prompt: What is roaming?
chosen: The process of a client passing between BSSs in an ESS, switching to an AP with a stronger signal as it moves.
rejected: The process of a client moving between two separate wireless networks with different SSIDs.

prompt: Who decides when a client roams to another AP?
chosen: The client device, which switches when its current AP's signal weakens and another is stronger.
rejected: The AP, which hands the client off when its signal drops below a threshold.

prompt: How much should AP cells overlap in an ESS?
chosen: About 10% to 15%, with some recommending 20%, so roaming is seamless without loss of connectivity.
rejected: About 50%, so a client is always in range of at least two APs.

prompt: What channels should neighbouring BSSs in an ESS use?
chosen: Non-overlapping channels, such as the 1-6-11 pattern in the 2.4 GHz band.
rejected: The same channel, so clients do not have to retune when they roam.

prompt: What is an MBSS?
chosen: A mesh basic service set, which connects multiple APs wirelessly so they can relay data to the distribution system without each needing a wired connection.
rejected: A multiple basic service set, where one AP advertises several SSIDs at once.

prompt: When is an MBSS useful?
chosen: Where running an Ethernet cable to each AP is impractical or too costly.
rejected: Where a single AP does not have enough radios to serve all the clients.

prompt: What is a RAP?
chosen: A root access point, an AP in an MBSS that is connected to the distribution system.
rejected: A relay access point, an AP that forwards frames between two other APs.

prompt: What is a MAP?
chosen: A mesh access point, an AP in an MBSS that is not connected to the distribution system.
rejected: A managed access point, one controlled by a wireless LAN controller.

prompt: How many radios should an MBSS AP ideally have?
chosen: Two on different channels: one providing a BSS for clients and one relaying frames over the mesh.
rejected: One, tuned to the mesh channel, since clients connect through the root AP.

prompt: Can a single-radio AP join an MBSS?
chosen: Yes, but with greatly reduced performance, since the one radio has to do both jobs.
rejected: No. A mesh AP requires at least two radios to function.

prompt: What is an AP in repeater mode?
chosen: An AP that takes the signal from a main AP and retransmits it to extend coverage beyond the main AP's cell.
rejected: An AP that copies the main AP's configuration so clients can connect to either one.

prompt: How does a repeater AP differ from a mesh AP?
chosen: A repeater is typically a standalone device extending one AP's range, while a mesh AP intelligently routes traffic through the best path in a web of APs.
rejected: A repeater relays frames at Layer 2 while a mesh AP routes them at Layer 3.

prompt: What is the downside of a repeater AP?
chosen: It occupies additional airtime for each packet it retransmits, reducing the network's overall throughput.
rejected: It requires its own wired connection to the distribution system.

prompt: What is a workgroup bridge?
chosen: An AP that connects a wired device without wireless capabilities to a wireless LAN, acting as a client of a main AP on that device's behalf.
rejected: An AP that bridges two wireless LANs together so their clients can communicate.

prompt: How does a wired device connect to a WGB?
chosen: Via an Ethernet cable.
rejected: Via a USB wireless adapter supplied with the WGB.

prompt: Can a WGB support more than one wired device?
chosen: Yes, but if the main AP is not a Cisco AP, the WGB must operate in Universal WGB mode, which supports only a single wired device.
rejected: No. A WGB can only ever act on behalf of one wired device.

prompt: What is an outdoor bridge?
chosen: An AP mode that connects separate LANs wirelessly over long distances, avoiding the cost of laying cable between buildings.
rejected: An AP mode that provides wireless coverage to outdoor areas such as courtyards.

prompt: What antennas do outdoor bridges use?
chosen: Directional antennas, which focus the signal so its strength is maintained over longer distances.
rejected: Omnidirectional antennas, so the link works regardless of how the APs are aimed.

prompt: What topologies can outdoor bridges use?
chosen: Point-to-point between two sites, or point-to-multipoint with several sites connecting to a central one.
rejected: Only point-to-point, since a directional antenna can aim at just one target.

prompt: What condition is essential for a long outdoor bridge link?
chosen: A clear line of sight between the two APs.
rejected: Both APs being tuned to the 2.4 GHz band for better penetration.
